title: Cover Story: Playing the long game at Forest City
body: Cover Story: Playing the long game at Forest City This article first appeared in City & Country, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026 It was a scorching afternoon when Country Garden Pacificview Sdn Bhd (CGPV) executive director and chief of regional industrial business development Kevin Li and regional vice-president Syarul Izam Sarifudin arrived at The Edge’s office in Petaling Jaya, Selangor. The pair had flown in from Johor Bahru to give an update on Forest City, a high-profile project in Johor that has dealt with some hot issues since its inception. “What we achieved [since 2015] up to 2025 was merely concentrating more on our operational stability, resource integration and preparing for our next phase of growth,” says Syarul. “In the early years, we were primarily viewed as a residential real estate developer. But we are now embarking into a new sector — managing townships and driving actual economic nodes of financial and industrial development in southern Johor.” The master developer of Forest City is a joint venture between China-headquartered developer Country Garden Holdings Co Ltd and Esplanade Danga 88 Sdn Bhd. Operating as an independent local management unit under Country Garden Malaysia’s executive umbrella, CGPV is responsible for Forest City’s master plan development and management, industrial park development and Special Financial Zone (SFZ) operation. Officially launched by the Malaysian government with duty-free island status in 2016, the 7,500-acre integrated development covers four reclaimed man-made islands over 5,000 acres and 2,500 acres on the mainland. Located in Iskandar Puteri, it sits along the Straits of Johor near the Malaysia-Singapore Second Link, just 2km across the water from Singapore. The ambitious development has made international headlines over the years, some of them for the wrong reasons, especially since it has fallen short of market expectations in terms of progress, sales and occupancy rates. These challenges were compounded by the Covid-19 pandemic and the well-documented financial restructuring of its parent company amid China’s broader real estate liquidity crisis. “When China’s property market faced a systemic downturn, amplified by global supply chain disruptions, macroeconomic shifts and strict pandemic controls, Country Garden — once China’s top property developer — was caught in the crossfire, just like many other big players in the country. However, late last year, our parent group successfully executed onshore and offshore debt restructurings in China,” says Li, who is also the chief financial officer of Country Garden Malaysia. Regardless of the situation faced by its parent company, he highlights that Country Garden Malaysia operates with complete operational and financial independence. “Since Country Garden entered Malaysia as its first overseas destination back in 2010 and 2011, the local operation has relied on an independent management team. For the past three years, our cash flow has been generated entirely within the country, allowing us to remain self-sustaining in terms of liquidity and debt servicing,” he says, adding that all five of its projects in the Klang Valley and Johor are performing steadily. According to Li, Country Garden Malaysia’s sales and cash collection was RM1.3 billion in 2023, more than RM1.1 billion in 2024, and RM1.3 billion in 2025. “More crucially, we utilised our local cash flows to fully settle bank borrowings and capital market obligations worth about RM2 billion over the past three years, including a RM1 billion sukuk … As at earlier this year, the remaining outstanding amount [of the sukuk] was only RM150 million. We pre-repaid them as our cash flow was comfortable.” With most of its debts cleared, local rating agency RAM upgraded Country Garden Malaysia’s outlook rating from negative to stable in March, reflecting its balance-sheet resilience despite global sector volatility. That financial stability has been supported by developments on the legal front. Malaysian courts have recently upheld the validity of sales and purchase agreements in favour of the developer. Dismissing buyer suits seeking to void contracts for reasons such as media portrayals of the project as a “ghost town”, the courts established that market downturns and post-purchase regret do not constitute grounds for breach. The decisions shield CGPV against speculative contract cancellations and protect its revenue base. “Forest City has completed and delivered 26,000 residential units so far. We understand that we cannot make every single person happy, and it is normal to receive feedback or complaints. We respect the buyers’ legal rights,” Li says. “But we also have our internal KPIs [key performance indicators] to meet. We are pleased to share that customer satisfaction consistently hits above 95% in our surveys and polls. Generally, the majority of our 20,000 residents are happy to live here, or they wouldn’t choose to continue staying. This is evidenced by our growing population.” A city waking up Today, Forest City is home to around 20,000 people living in 66 completed blocks, over 770 acres of the approved 5,000-acre reclaimed island land bank. “If you pass by from Iskandar Puteri towards Batam, you can see the lights on across the residential towers at night,” Syarul says. “It is a night-and-day difference compared with what people experienced immediately after the pandemic in early 2021.” Demographics have shifted significantly, he adds. While buyers were once predominantly mainland Chinese, the current resident base is largely local Malaysians, many of whom commute daily to Singapore or work in nearby industrial parks, as well as expatriates of different nationalities. “The township’s commercial pulse is also quickening,” says Syarul. “The Fisherman’s Wharf commercial street has seen steady footfall, with duty-free shops, eateries and premier banking facilities, including branches of Maybank and CIMB, with Affin Bank and AmBank joining the fold soon.” Forest City attracts between 1.5 million and two million tourists annually. Its crown jewel is Forest City Golf Resort, located on the mainland about 9km from the man-made islands. Featuring two 18-hole international championship courses, it draws golfers from Japan, South Korea and Singapore. There is also an affordable beachfront water park that offers weekend entertainment for visiting families. “Forest City is probably the only sandy beach in Johor Bahru. Otherwise, you have to go to Desaru, which is an hour away. To draw more visitors, we are also collaborating with some watersports academies on courses for adults and children. The beach and water park are very popular during school holidays and weekends, contributing to our growing annual tourist and visitor numbers,” Syarul says. Meanwhile, Network School, a start-up society and experimental community based on Silicon Valley entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan’s book The Network State, was set up in the township in October 2024. Balaji’s private co-living and co-working hub at Marina Hotel drew hundreds of international digital nomads, crypto enthusiasts and tech workers. However, in July 2026, the Iskandar Puteri City Council (MBIP) revoked the Network School operator’s business licence for breaching local licensing conditions. The management of the school clarified that CGPV operates solely as a commercial landlord, and that the developer is fully cooperating with the local authorities to ensure all commercial tenants adhere to the regulatory framework. Strategic shift Li says while Forest City’s master plan is unchanged, CGPV is shifting its focus towards commercial and industrial developments, in alignment with the government’s broader economic development plan for the state. “We maintain the master plan as it is because, to us, it is still a very fantastic plan even after a decade. Of course, for such a mega development, you have to do it in phases, and there will be small twists and adjustments in between. But overall, we do not have plans to review the master plan. Now, we are embarking on the third phase of development. We foresee the entire master plan being completed only by 2040. It is now 12% to 13% developed,” says Syarul. The biggest “twists and adjustments” to the master plan were its integration into the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) and designation as an SFZ. In August 2023, the government announced that Forest City would be designated as an SFZ to boost foreign investment, with incentives such as a 15% income tax rate for skilled workers and lower business operating costs. A year later, the government launched the tax incentive framework for the SFZ, which includes a zero tax rate for single family offices (SFO), a 5% corporate tax rate for fintech and global business services, and concessionary income tax rates. In early 2025, Malaysia and Singapore signed a bilateral agreement to establish the JS-SEZ. Under the agreement, Forest City was formally incorporated as Flagship G, one of nine primary flagship zones within the 3,505 sq km economic zone. “We started [the master plan] with residential and, maybe, this made people misunderstand that Forest City is focusing on high-rise residential developments. The SFZ designation puts us right back on track to [industrial projects],” says Li. “Under the SFZ blueprint, the development is divided into two distinct functional zones, where the island component acts as a core financial services hub, focusing on single-family offices, fintech, foreign payment operating systems and back-office financial services. Meanwhile, the mainland focuses on smart logistics, high-tech manufacturing and global business services.” To encourage direct investments in Forest City, the Malaysian government established the Iskandar Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor (IMFC-J) at Forest City’s 42-storey primary office tower, Menara Delima Satu, to streamline the investment process. The centre houses 18 government agencies under one roof and acts as a single processing point for foreign investors. “A key cornerstone of the SFZ is attracting family offices. The SC (Securities Commission) set an AUM (assets under management) threshold of RM30 million for family offices setting up in Forest City, a far more accessible entry point compared with Singapore’s S$15 million (RM47.9 million) requirement or Hong Kong’s HK$240 million (RM124.7 million) benchmark,” Li says. Syarul stresses, however, that Malaysia is not competing with Singapore or Hong Kong in the SFO segment but is instead complementing them. “It is about synergy. Under the SFZ rules, family offices in Forest City can invest up to 90% of their AUM globally. This means that investors can set up their operational base here in Forest City at one-third to one-fourth of the operational cost, while still leveraging Singapore’s capital markets just across the strait. It is very attractive to many family offices,” he explains. Under the SFO Incentive Scheme guidelines issued by the SC, it is mandatory to establish a physical office in Forest City to qualify for and maintain SC approval and the accompanying 0% tax incentive. According to Li, over 40 SFOs have secured physical office space in Forest City, with nine having formally received SC approval to date. “We are very positive about this, though we do not have an actual target of having many of them in Forest City in the near future because it is beyond our control and SC has its plan. But it is a strong catalyst in helping to add vibrancy to Forest City because when the offices come, they bring in their professional teams — accountants, lawyers and finance and investment experts,” he adds. Forest City is also targeting global business services. CGPV is in advanced discussions with two major international banking institutions — one looking to relocate its back-office operations from Singapore, and another expanding its operational footprint from Kuala Lumpur. Forest City 2.0 Despite the tailwinds from the SFZ, Li and Syarul acknowledge that transforming the mega project into a self-sustaining regional economy is not without immediate, real-world hurdles. The most pressing challenge currently is cross-border physical connectivity and accessibility. “While the project is geographically proximate to Singapore, seamlessly moving people, goods and daily commuters across borders remains a complex, multi-jurisdictional effort,” says Li. “Furthermore, regional competition from peers like Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam means that Malaysia must continually sharpen its execution speed and policy delivery to stay ahead.” To close this connectivity gap, Country Garden is taking interim measures while lobbying government authorities for long-term infrastructure approvals. “Before all the major government infrastructure projects are completed, we are bridging the gap ourselves. We currently run daily direct shuttles transferring residents and workers to the Sultan Abu Bakar CIQ Second Link complex,” Li says. For the long term, the developer has submitted plans to the joint Malaysia-Singapore ministerial committee under the Iskandar Regional Development Authority (IRDA) for a dedicated ferry terminal. Once approved, ferry routes will connect Forest City directly to Raffles Marina in Singapore and Batam in Indonesia. “We are also asking the government for assistance to permit a direct highway connection linking straight to Tuas, and to integrate Forest City into upcoming regional rail routes like the RTS [Rapid Transit System], ART [Automated Rapid Transit] and transport corridors heading to Kulai and Senai,” he adds. “Moving people efficiently is crucial to unlocking the full value of the JS-SEZ but because these are country-to-country matters, we have to keep pushing and following up continuously.” Simultaneously, the master developer is pivoting to boosting population density and creating high-value local jobs, away from traditional residential property sales, towards what the team calls “Forest City 2.0”. “We are not launching any more residential projects in the near future, but focusing on clearing the inventory. We will advance commercial and industrial land development earlier than originally scheduled to inject immediate economic vibrancy,” Li says. “Our next focus is to bring in companies and industries to invest or establish their presence here.” Acknowledging the importance of generating sufficient jobs to increase Forest City’s population, CGPV is actively trying to draw data centres, logistics players and manufacturers to its upcoming 418-acre industrial park. “We need to create real economic dynamics. If you don’t generate jobs and economic substance, you cannot sustain a population,” Li stresses. The response to this industrial shift has been positive. In the first half of this year alone, the developer logged over 300 company enquiries and secured a 40-acre industrial land deal with a manufacturer in Phase 1 of the industrial park, paving the way for ready-built factory developments in Phase 2 should market demand sustain. In another strategic partnership, Country Garden recently signed a term sheet with Penang-based Oriental Holdings Bhd (KL:ORIENT) to develop a RM750 million healthcare hub in Forest City, anchored by a 500-bed hospital alongside comprehensive medical supply chain services. “Internationally, we are actively introducing Forest City to big-name [multinational corporations]. It is not so much for their name, but the entire supply chain. We are looking to bring in ‘queen bee’ investors,” Li says. “We have been doing roadshows, especially in China, to introduce the JS-SEZ and Forest City SFZ. We went to Shenzhen and Suzhou, which have some of the most successful industrial parks in China.” Apart from the industrial park, CGPV has also received enquiries from international investors interested in private island parcels. “It is something that we are looking at. Instead of standard residential towers, we can custom-reclaim approved island plots, such as 1.5 to two acres, based entirely on an investor’s specific operational or residential requirements. It’s about being adaptive to what the current market actually demands,” he says. Road to 2030 and beyond Apart from Forest City, Country Garden Malaysia has four other major developments in Johor and the Klang Valley, executed largely through JVs. “Out of our five projects in Malaysia, four are structured as JVs,” Li explains. “Only Danga Bay is 100% held by Country Garden Malaysia. We welcome JVs because local partners bring value to the table, though for master site design, we prefer to lead.” In Johor Bahru, Country Garden Central Park has completed three phases comprising over 3,000 residential units that are nearly fully sold. The developer is now planning subsequent sub-phases over a 10- to 12-year development cycle. In Kuala Lumpur, the initial two phases of township development Lake City in Taman Wahyu are completed and sold out, with Phase 3 scheduled for launch next year. The remaining four parcels have been earmarked for development over a 15-year period. In Semenyih, Selangor, residential development Diamond City launched its final landed parcel in September 2025, which is expected to wrap up construction within two years. With a substantial land bank in its existing portfolio, the developer will focus its resources on executing its active pipeline over the next decade. As the interview draws to a close, both Li and Syarul reflect on the long-term nature of master township development. “Rome was not built in a day,” Li says. “When we first came to this coastal area in Johor, it was completely rural. Today, the infrastructure is firmly established. Development never moves in a straight upward line; it moves in spirals, but it always moves forward. “We wish the public to know that since the first day Country Garden has been here in Malaysia, we have wanted to be here long term. Of course, there are twists and turns over the years, but we cannot deny the contribution of the company in Malaysia.” He says Country Garden has invested RM32 billion in Malaysia, including RM20 billion in Forest City alone. “We have created jobs, contributed to the country’s tax revenues and trained local skilled workers. Most importantly, after so many challenges and uncertainties, we were here, and we are still here today. The fundamentals are in place, and we have absolute faith in what Forest City will become.” Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. title: A Reformasi government that arrests reformasi activists?
body: Kua Kia Soong Malaysia now has a Reformasi government arresting Reformasi activists. On 22 September, Amir Hariri Abdul Hadi, executive director of youth-led NGO Mandiri, and Dobby Chew, its finance director, were arrested under the anti-money-laundering law Amla after voluntarily presenting themselves to police to assist an investigation. They were remanded for three days and released on 24 September. Police say the investigation concerns suspected unlawful funds and that five bank accounts have been frozen. No, they are not podcasters. The podcasters came earlier. On 6 August, Brian Kong of Let’s Get It Podcast and Shamsul Saad of The Gut Shot Podcast were arrested and remanded for two days over an episode ‘Malaysia introduced me to racism’, which police said raised racial and religious sensitivities. They were investigated under the Sedition Act, Penal Code and Communications and Multimedia Act. So here we are. Activists arrested. Podcasters arrested. Human rights defenders investigated. Civil society bank accounts frozen. And this is supposed to be the government born of Reformasi. Perhaps the slogan has undergone a little institutional reform itself: - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member Reformasi – formerly a movement against the machinery of repression. Reformasi 2.0 – now operating the machinery. The joke would be complete if the government announced that the next Reformasi rally will be held at the nearest police lock-up. The question for the former reformers This is where I would particularly like to hear from those who once stood on the other side of the barricades. Adam Adli was a student activist who became a symbol of youthful dissent before entering government. He is now deputy higher education minister. Fahmi Fadzil, once associated with the Reformasi generation, is now communications minister – the very portfolio intimately connected with freedom of expression and the regulation of online speech. Parliament records him as the minister responsible for the communications and multimedia legislation. So, gentlemen, a simple question: Where are your red lines? Is there a point at which the arrest of activists becomes unacceptable? A point at which the detention of journalists or podcasters becomes intolerable? A point at which laws inherited from the old order are used so aggressively that you say: “Enough. This is not the Reformasi we fought for”? And if that point exists, what is it? Is there a line beyond which you would resign in protest rather than remain in office and defend the indefensible? Or has entering government produced a miraculous transformation in political eyesight – where the handcuffs that once looked oppressive from the outside suddenly look perfectly reasonable from the inside? This is not a question about party loyalty. It is a question of principle. The great Reformasi rinse cycle Malaysia has seen this movie before. First comes the noble language: Reform. Justice. Democracy. Freedom. Rule of law. Then comes power. Then comes the discovery that the laws used against one’s opponents are actually rather useful. And finally comes the most beautiful phrase in the administrative vocabulary: “Let the authorities do their job.” Of course, the authorities must investigate genuine criminal allegations. But democracy requires another job to be done as well: the government must restrain the machinery of the state when that machinery threatens legitimate civil society, freedom of expression and political dissent. The UN special rapporteur on human rights defenders has already urged the Malaysian authorities to halt measures that misuse anti-money-laundering or anti-terrorism laws to harass or unduly restrict human rights defenders. Several international rights organisations likewise raised due process and chilling effect concerns over the crackdow on Mandiri and Hayat. These are not trivial questions. In a democracy, remand is not conviction. But deprivation of liberty is still deprivation of liberty. Perhaps the greatest irony is that many of today’s government politicians once understood this perfectly. They knew that democracy was not simply about winning elections. They knew that civil society had to be free to criticise the government. They knew that dissent was not treason. They knew that activists were not enemies of the state. So what happened? Did Reformasi finally succeed – only to discover that the former rebels had become the establishment? Or did the establishment simply swallow Reformasi whole? There is an old political warning: Power does not necessarily corrupt. Sometimes it merely reveals whether your principles were conditional on not having power. That is why the question to the former Reformasi activists now in government is so simple: What are your red lines? If an activist is arrested, what will make you speak? If a podcaster is detained, what will make you act? If freedom of expression is curtailed, what will make you resign? If the laws once used against you are now being used against the next generation of activists, how many arrests will it take before you say: “This is no longer Reformasi”? If there are no red lines, perhaps Malaysians should stop calling this a Reformasi government. Perhaps it is simply another government that has discovered the comfortable side of power. And perhaps the most appropriate Reformasi slogan for Malaysia in 2026 is: ‘Reformasi – please report to the lock-up.’ Dr Kua Kia Soong, a former MP, is the director of human rights group Suaram. title: Jual saham SD Guthrie susulan penerbitan sukuk PNB tidak wajar – Maybank IB | DagangNews - Berita Bisnes Anda
body: KUALA LUMPUR 15 Sept - Maybank Investment Bank (Maybank IB) menyifatkan penjualan saham SD Guthrie Bhd susulan penerbitan sukuk boleh tukar (ES) oleh Permodalan Nasional Bhd (PNB) sebagai keterlaluan dan tidak wajar. Menurut firma penyelidikan itu asas SD Guthrie kekal utuh meskipun harga sahamnya mengalami tekanan baru-baru ini. Tambahnya, reaksi pasaran terhadap penerbitan ES bernilai AS$300 juta atau RM1.22 bilion oleh PNB adalah tidak berasas kerana instrumen berkenaan tidak memberi kesan kepada pendapatan sesaham (EPS) SD Guthrie. “Kami percaya penjualan saham baru-baru ini adalah tidak wajar kerana tiada perubahan fundamental yang berlaku sepanjang bulan lalu selain penerbitan sukuk boleh tukar AS$300 juta oleh PNB,” katanya dalam nota penyelidikan pada Selasa. Sehubungan itu Maybank IB menaik taraf penarafan SD Guthrie kepada “BELI” daripada “PEGANG”. Disalah tafsir pasaran Maybank IB berkata kebimbangan mengenai potensi tekanan jualan atau lebihan bekalan saham daripada sukuk boleh tukar itu juga telah berakhir dan sebahagian besarnya disalah tafsir oleh pasaran. Ini kerana sukuk tersebut diterbitkan oleh PNB, bukannya SD Guthrie, justeru tiada saham baharu akan diterbitkan oleh kumpulan itu sekiranya pelabur melaksanakan hak penukaran mereka. Selain itu, Maybank IB menganggarkan harga saham SD Guthrie perlu meningkat kepada sekurang-kurangnya RM8.66 sebelum pelabur sukuk boleh menukarkan pegangan mereka kepada saham SD Guthrie. Paras itu jauh lebih tinggi berbanding harga dagangan semasa saham berkenaan. Saham SD Guthrie meningkat daripada RM6.14 pada 9 September, ketika PNB mengumumkan penerbitan sukuk boleh tukar itu, kepada RM6.34 pada Selasa, memberikan kumpulan perladangan itu permodalan pasaran sebanyak RM43.85 bilion. Peningkatan penarafan itu turut disokong prospek pendapatan SD Guthrie yang kekal kukuh. Untung dijangka meningkat Maybank IB mengunjurkan keuntungan bersih teras kumpulan sebanyak RM2.9 bilion bagi tahun kewangan berakhir 31 Disember 2026, iaitu 5% lebih tinggi berbanding konsensus pasaran sebanyak RM2.76 bilion. Bagaimanapun, firma itu berkata jangkaan konsensus pasaran bagi tempoh jangka panjang masih lebih tinggi berbanding unjurannya. Berdasarkan data Bloomberg, sentimen pasaran terhadap SD Guthrie kekal positif dengan 14 daripada 18 firma penyelidikan memberikan penarafan “BELI”, dua “PEGANG” dan dua lagi “OUTPERFORM”. Harga sasaran konsensus Bloomberg bagi tempoh 12 bulan pula ialah RM7.65, membayangkan potensi kenaikan sebanyak 20.9% daripada paras dagangan semasa. Maybank IB mengekalkan harga sasaran RM7.10 terhadap SD Guthrie, berdasarkan 0.55 kali nilai aset bersih disemak (RNAV). Firma itu menjangkakan pertumbuhan masa depan kumpulan akan semakin disokong oleh perniagaan baharu, termasuk pembangunan bersama taman perindustrian melibatkan lebih 20,000 ekar tanah. Perniagaan tersebut disasarkan untuk menjana pendapatan tahunan antara RM500 juta hingga RM700 juta. Selain itu, SD Guthrie turut menyasarkan pembangunan projek solar berskala besar berkapasiti satu gigawatt, sekali gus membuka ruang kepada sumber pertumbuhan baharu di luar perniagaan perladangan tradisional.

title: Allianz, Hong Leong Bank Lead Bursa Losers As Selling Pressure Dominates
body: Allianz Malaysia Bhd and Hong Leong Bank Bhd led Bursa Malaysia’s decliners at the close of trading session on Sept 11, as selling pressure remained broad with 809 losers outnumbering 427 gainers.  Allianz was the top loser, sliding 56 sen to RM21.12, followed by Hong Leong Bank, which fell 52 sen to RM23.08. Sunway Construction Group Bhd dropped 47 sen to RM7.44, while Fraser & Neave Holdings Bhd lost 44 sen to RM23.56 and ViTrox Corp Bhd declined 32 sen to RM9.15.  The weaker breadth underscored cautious sentiment across the market, with 474 counters unchanged, 1,121 untraded and 32 suspended at 5pm.  On the upside, Petronas Chemicals Group Bhd topped the list, rising 27 sen to RM5.09. Eurospan Holdings Bhd advanced 18 sen to RM3.15, while Batu Kawan Bhd and Concrete Engineering Products Bhd each added 12 sen, closing at RM20.16 and RM4 respectively.  Mega Fortris Bhd rounded out the top five gainers, climbing nine sen to RM2.40.  Total market turnover stood at 3.57 billion units worth RM3.28 billion compared to 3.98 billion units valued at RM3.14 billion on Sept 10.

title: MHC reschedules Deepavali Day matches after public backlash
body: KUALA LUMPUR: The public are annoyed and are questioning why Malaysian Hockey League (MHL) matches will be played on Nov 8, Deepavali Day. The second round of MHL started on Monday, and two matches, Terengganu Hockey Team against Armed Forces and TNB Thunderbolts against Maybank, will be held on Nov 8. Both matches are to be played at TNB Stadium in Bangi. Malaysian Hockey Confederation (MHC) chief executive officer V. Jayanandhan, when contacted, said that they are aware of it. "The two MHL hockey matches scheduled on Nov 8 will be changed to another date. I have already informed the MHL tournament director Dalit Singh," said Jayanandhan. "The Terengganu Hockey Team's match against Armed Forces will be played on Nov 9 while the match between TNB Thunderbolts and Maybank will be played on Nov 14.: League leaders Tenaga Nasional (TNB) were unhappy with the fixtures, as they have to play Forces on Wednesday with only 11 players having arrived from Japan on Monday after playing in the Asian Games. Daljit said they would make changes to the fixtures so that TNB's match against Forces will be played on another date. Clubs have to release national players for the six-nation Asian Champions Trophy in Punjab, India from Oct 27 to Nov 5 while the national league will continue during the tournament. This will affect clubs that won't have the services of national players in the MHL during the period. Officials need to be more professional in organising the MHL, as the national league is in haywire.

title: A record earnings run
body: This article first appeared in The Edge Malaysia Weekly on October 5, 2026 - October 11, 2026 CIMB Group Holdings Bhd Despite an increasingly challenging banking landscape, CIMB Group Holdings Bhd (KL:CIMB) has continued to set new earnings benchmarks, hitting a record net profit in 2024 before surpassing it with a fresh record in 2025. Net profit at the country’s second largest banking group and Asean’s fifth largest by assets rose 1.7% to RM7.86 billion in the financial year ended Dec 31, 2025 (FY2025), from RM7.73 billion a year earlier. That followed a 10.7% increase in FY2024 and a much sharper 28.3% jump in FY2023 to RM6.98 billion. The steady rise in earnings translated into a risk-weighted compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 19.6% over the three years — the highest among its peers. This made CIMB this year’s winner of The Edge Billion Ringgit Club (BRC) award for Highest growth in profit after tax over three years in the financial services sector, among banks that have a market capitalisation of at least RM10 billion. It also won in the BRC Super Big Cap category for companies with a market capitalisation of above RM40 billion. It is the third year running that CIMB has won in both categories, marking how far the group has come since the Covid-19 pandemic. Its return on equity (ROE) improved from 10.7% in 2023 to 11.2% in 2024 and 11.3% in 2025, from just 9% in 2022. Thanks to its strong share price appreciation and attractive dividends, CIMB also clinched this year’s award for highest returns to shareholders over three years in the Super Big Cap category for companies with a market cap of over RM40 billion. CIMB’s shareholder returns grew at a CAGR of 20.2% over the three years — ahead of the competition — as its share price shot up to RM7.55 on March 31, 2026, from RM4.35 on March 31, 2023. The returns reflect the higher dividends that shareholders received as profits grew. CIMB increased its dividend per share from 43 sen in 2023 to 47 sen in 2024, before declaring 47.1 sen for FY2025. Each year’s payout included a special dividend of seven sen per share. The latest payout amounted to a record of about RM5.1 billion. Supporting its share price is the fact that the group has committed to returning up to RM2 billion of additional capital to shareholders by 2027 through special dividends and/or share buybacks, subject to market conditions and regulatory approvals. This year, given a more challenging macroeconomic backdrop, including a prolonged conflict in the Middle East macroeconomics, CIMB’s 1HFY2026 financial performance softened from the previous corresponding period. Net profit for the period fell a marginal 0.2% year on year (y-o-y) to RM3.85 billion, while revenue slid to RM10.97 billion from RM11.10 billion. Be that as it may, it delivered an annualised ROE of 11%, in line with its target of 11% to 11.5% for the full year. It announced an all-cash first interim dividend of 19.65 sen per share, based on a consistent payout ratio of 55.5%, which translated into a total dividend payout of RM2.1 billion. Notably, asset quality remained broadly stable, with its gross impaired loan ratio at an all-time low of 1.6% at end-June, compared with 1.7% three months earlier. Group CEO Novan Amirudin said the execution momentum for Forward30 — the group’s six-year strategic programme that started running from last year — remained firmly on track. “Our destination is clear: to become the top-of-mind Asean bank by 2030. To get there, we must deliver a sustainable ROE of 12% to 13% by 2027 and compete consistently in the top quartile of our regional peers by 2030,” he said in the group’s latest annual report. Nevertheless, headwinds persist, and the group expects funding cost pressures in Indonesia and competition on loan repricing to weigh on its net interest margin (NIM) this year. CIMB’s NIM stood at 2.04% in 2QFY2026, down four basis points from the previous quarter and down 11bps on a y-o-y basis. A notable development this year is that CIMB’s Thai unit, CIMB Thai Bank, was delisted from the Stock Exchange of Thailand on Sept 12, more than 2½ years after a regulatory process triggered by stricter free-float requirements. CIMB Thai remains a core subsidiary and the delisting is not expected to have a material impact on the lender. The Thai unit is profitable, having posted more than a fivefold y-o-y increase in net profit to THB886.3 million in 2QFY2026. As at Aug 28, CIMB’s share price closed at RM7.96, giving the company a market value of RM86.05 billion. Bloomberg data shows 15 “buy” and five “hold” recommendations on the stock, with no “sell” calls. The 12-month average target price was RM8.88. “CIMB has balance sheet flexibility to navigate NIM pressure, and loan loss coverage buffers to weather any asset quality turbulence,” AmInvestment Bank Research said in a Sept 1 report. “The bank has also consistently proved itself as a strong strategy executor and good capital allocator. Besides, we like CIMB’s stance on returning excess capital, with scope for more beyond the planned RM2 billion programme, especially when its dividend payout ratio is about 10 percentage points below larger peers.” Save by subscribing to us for your print and/or digital copy. title: Maybank, Gallant Venture to develop Bintan halal hub
body: KUALA LUMPUR: Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank) has teamed up with Gallant Venture to develop the Bintan Inti Halal Hub (BIHH), a halal industrial ecosystem in Bintan, Indonesia amid growing global demand for halal products and services. The collaboration brings together Maybank's regional banking and halal ecosystem expertise with Gallant's industrial infrastructure to create opportunities for businesses looking to expand across Asean's growing halal economy. Maybank will provide a comprehensive suite of Islamic banking and financial solutions to businesses operating within BIHH and across the broader halal value chain. "This includes account services, deposits, cash management solutions, foreign exchange services, trade and working capital financing, payroll and settlement solutions, as well as access to Maybank's regional network and Islamic banking expertise," the bank said in a statement. The hub will support businesses expanding across Indonesia, Singapore and Malaysia, while attracting international investment into regional manufacturing and trading operations. Businesses will also gain access to halal certification support, business matching, strategic partners and Salaam Marketplace, Malaysia's first B2B halal marketplace, which expanded to Singapore in November 2025. Maybank Islamic Bhd group chief executive officer of Islamic banking and Maybank Islamic Bhd chief executive officer Yasin Abdullah said the initiative strengthens the ecosystem needed to help businesses connect, grow and tap into regional halal trade opportunities. He said the halal economy was among the fastest-growing segments globally, presenting significant opportunities for businesses across Southeast Asia. "This initiative also supports our ROAR30 aspirations - powering the real economy, opening up RM100 billion in opportunities for small and medium enterprise, and building the foundations for Maybank's global Islamic leadership. "By bringing together financing, market access, industry partnerships and halal ecosystem capabilities, we aim to support businesses throughout their expansion journey and contribute meaningfully to Asean's halal economy," he added.

title: DNB completes RM5.2bil financing to support next phase of 5G growth
body: KUALA LUMPUR: Digital Nasional Bhd (DNB) has completed a RM5.2bil syndicated Islamic term financing, strengthening its long-term funding position as Malaysia moves into the next phase of its dual 5G network framework. In a statement, DNB said the financing will facilitate the planned exit of Minister of Finance Inc (MOF Inc) as an ordinary shareholder and the transition to equal ownership among its mobile network operator shareholders, namely CelcomDigi Bhd, Maxis Broadband Sdn Bhd and YTL Power International Bhd. The ownership transition is expected in the early fourth quarter of 2026, while MOF Inc will retain a special share in DNB to safeguard national interests. The syndicated financing also includes the refinancing of DNB's government-guaranteed revolving credit facility, which expired on Sept 29, and establishes a longer-term funding structure to support the company's growth. DNB said the completion of the financing coincided with the award of the full 100 MHz of the 3.3–3.4 GHz spectrum and the conversion of its entire 240 MHz spectrum holding to a spectrum assignment. The assignment by the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) takes effect from Oct 1. DNB said the 240 MHz spectrum block would enhance network capacity, efficiency and performance and support technologies including Massive MIMO, carrier aggregation, 5G Advanced and artificial intelligence-driven network capabilities. Chief executive officer Datuk Azman Ismail said the financing would provide DNB with a sustainable platform to operate independently while continuing to invest in network enhancement and capacity expansion. “The successful completion of this RM5.2bil financing exercise marks a significant milestone for DNB and reflects strong confidence in our business fundamentals, operational track record and long-term role in Malaysia’s digital economy,” he said. Maybank Investment Bank Bhd acted as mandated lead arranger, bookrunner and coordinating arranger for the financing. AmInvestment Bank Bhd, CIMB Islamic Bank Bhd, RHB Islamic Bank Bhd and United Overseas Bank (Malaysia) Bhd were joint mandated lead arrangers, while AmInvestment Bank was DNB's financial adviser.

title: 丰隆银行3分行明年关闭，客户业务转移至附近分行！ - Newswav
body: 丰隆银行3分行明年关闭，客户业务转移至附近分行！ 丰隆银行（Hong Leong Bank）将关闭3家位于吉隆坡的分行，最后营业日定于2027年2月19日（星期五），受影响分行的客户及业务将转移至附近分行。 根据丰隆银行官网资料，3家即将关闭的分行分别位于Segambut、Brickfields及Pandan Indah。 3家分行将搬去哪？ 其中，Segambut分行关闭后，相关业务将转移至Menjalara分行；Brickfields分行的业务则转往Bangsar分行。 至于Pandan Indah分行，相关业务将转移至Ampang Taman Putra分行。 这意味着，受影响客户日后仍可继续通过丰隆银行其他分行办理相关业务，不过需要前往新的指定分行。 2月19日最后营业 上述3家分行的最后营业日为2027年2月19日（星期五）。 客户若平时习惯到这些分行办理银行业务，可留意相关安排，并在分行关闭后前往指定的替代分行。 银行也建议客户根据自身需要，提前熟悉新的服务地点，以免分行关闭后影响日常银行业务。 全国仍有逾200家分行 尽管这3家分行将关闭，丰隆银行在全国仍维持规模庞大的实体服务网络。 目前，丰隆银行在全国拥有超过200家分行及1025个自助服务机（ATM），客户仍可通过其他分行及自助服务渠道办理相关银行业务。 随着银行业持续推动数码化，越来越多客户通过网上银行及手机应用办理转账、缴费及其他日常银行业务，银行也持续根据客户使用情况调整实体分行网络。 因此，这次关闭3家分行主要涉及相关地点的服务网络调整，客户的银行账户及业务并不会因为分行关闭而终止。

title: Asia Among Most Vulnerable to AI Correction, Asean Unit Warns
body: (Oct 5): Southeast Asia plus China, Japan and South Korea are more at risk than most economies to any potential collapse in the artificial-intelligence boom, which could trigger shocks across financial markets and the real economy. The region is “particularly exposed” because it’s at the centre of global AI supply chains and “increasingly integrated into AI-related financial markets,” the Asean+3 Macroeconomic Research Office said in its 2026 Financial Stability Report published on Monday. “A disorderly correction could therefore propagate through multiple channels — including lower technology exports, portfolio losses, capital outflows, refinancing pressure on leveraged technology and infrastructure firms, and weaker investor confidence,” it said. The report comes amid growing investor concern about the AI boom, including the high valuation of tech companies, the surge in spending on chips and data centres, and circular financing deals in which companies appear to be funding each other. Tech-related exports have been helping Asia withstand the impact of high energy prices and US tariffs. Much of the physical production in the technology cycle takes place in Asia, from memory chips in South Korea to semiconductor assembly in Malaysia. The region accounted for two-thirds of the growth in global AI-related trade, Amro said. Should AI demand suddenly fall short, a pullback in capital spending would undermine export revenues, investments and broader economic growth. Some regional equity markets are also heavily concentrated on AI, such as South Korea, exposing them to a sharp correction in prices. Other markets like Japan and Hong Kong have come to move closely in line with US AI and technology firms, meaning shocks could also be transmitted even absent a domestic trigger, according to Amro. As hyperscalers increasingly turn to borrowings to fund costly data centre buildouts, higher leverage could amplify shocks if AI returns disappoint, the report said. Opaque private credit markets and circular financing deals could worsen the instability. “A sharp correction in AI-related financial assets could spill over to the broader financial system through forced deleveraging and tighter credit conditions,” Amro said. Central bankers around the world, from the Bank of England to the Monetary Authority of Singapore, have increasingly raised concerns about whether massive AI investments can be sustainable. The technology has developed at breakneck speed, but stiff competition among developers, higher borrowing costs and growing pushback against data centres and AI’s security threats have raised concerns. title: 13th PropertyGuru Asia Awards Malaysia with iProperty honours real estate excellence |  Penang Property Talk
body: 13th PropertyGuru Asia Awards Malaysia with iProperty honours real estate excellence Top developers celebrated the 13th PropertyGuru Asia Awards Malaysia in partnership with iProperty, presented by Lim Soh & Goonting Advocates & Solicitors, at The St. Regis Kuala Lumpur. Guided by the theme “Defined by Excellence,” the 2026 PropertyGuru Asia Awards Malaysia with iProperty recognised the country’s best in real estate across 62 categories. From township developers to breakthrough companies, this year’s awards were comprehensive, honouring the best in different real estate segments and regions. Timber Land Group won the evening’s top honour, Best Developer, marking its first-ever win in the category, in addition to Best Developer (East Malaysia). CPI Land was named Best Developer (Central Malaysia) alongside award-winning project Tuan Straits. Tanah Sutera took both Best Developer (Southern Malaysia) and Best Landed Homes Developer, buoyed by winning project The Seed. JLand Group, named Best Township Developer, collected the most awards of any company, covering Developer, Development, and Design categories for projects including Arena Larkin; Bandar Tiram; Ibrahim Technopolis (IBTEC) – Aspiration Park; Ibrahim Technopolis (IBTEC) – STeP West; and Medora One. JRK Holdings Berhad won both Best Breakthrough Developer and Best Boutique Developer. Keck Seng (Malaysia) Berhad was named Best Mixed Use Developer, also winning for the project Daya 1 Residences, Taman Daya. Penang developers also made their mark at this year’s awards, with PTL Properties, Aspen and Pinnacle Group among the winners. PTL Properties was named Best Lifestyle Developer, with The Rimbun also winning Best Mass Market Landed Development (Northern) and Best Townhouse Development. Aspen’s Aspen Vision City received the Best Township Development (Northern) award, while Pinnacle Group won Best Premium High-Rise Development (Northern) for Pinnacle Bukit Gambier. Other companies with winning projects include Amalan Setar (M) Sdn Bhd, which won for Ixora Garden – Sari Alamanda 4 Phase 2; Armani Group (Armani Hallson Bukit Bintang); Astaka Kimlun Sdn Bhd (Amora Serviced Residence); BCB Land Sdn. Bhd. (Straya Heights); Coronade Properties Sdn Bhd (Coronation Square; Coronade Twins – Serviced Residences); CTC Development Malaysia Sdn Bhd (CTC Skyone @ Bukit Chagar); Faire Development (bée); Gunung Impian Development Sdn Bhd (Taman Impian Emas); Infra Park Sdn Bhd (MLIMA Kiara); KEB Berhad (Residensi Cove @ Kota Syahbandar); Matrix Concepts (Levia Residence Puchong); OCR Templer Sdn Bhd (D’Templer Hilltop Residences); Peter’s Group (Cherita Residences); Puncak Concept Sdn Bhd (Puncak LakePark City @ Cyberjaya); R&F Development Sdn Bhd (R&F Princess Cove); Steadfast Properties (Laguna Residences); Tiram Industrial Park Sdn Bhd (Akasia Business Park); Tropicana Corporation Berhad (Clarissa Serviced Suites, Tropicana Cenang); UEM Sunrise Berhad (Intrika, Serene Heightshase s); and Worldwide Holdings Berhad (Pavonia Worldwide, Bukit Bandaraya Shah Alam). Outstanding real estate figures The 13th PropertyGuru Asia Awards Malaysia with iProperty celebrated some of the impactful figures in Malaysian real estate. Tan Sri Dato’ Seri Dr. Jeffrey Cheah KBE AO, founder and chairman of Sunway Group, received the Life Achievement Award. Dato’ Seri Azmir Merican, group managing director and chief executive officer of Sime Darby Property, was named Real Estate Personality of the Year. Dato’ Sri Edwin Tan Pei Seng, executive chairman of Paragon Globe Berhad, was honoured as Rising Star, while Ms. Maggie Ng Mui Kit, chief executive officer of Kuok Group Property Division (Southern), received the Woman Changemaker Award. Consumers, catalysts, and consistency The Consumer Demand Award continued this year, recognising the property that captured the strongest genuine interest from Malaysian property seekers. Determined by consumer views and leads across PropertyGuru.com.my and iProperty.com.my, Leisure Farm Resort by Mulpha International was named Most In-Demand Bungalow/Villa, in addition to winning Best Resort-Style Township Development. The People’s Choice Awards also continued the tradition of tapping consumer opinion to identify the nation’s 10 favourite developers. This year, 15,383 votes were cast for developers that consumers in Malaysia admire and trust. The winners of the People’s Choice Awards in 2026 are: Berinda Group; Coronade Properties Sdn Bhd; CPI Land; Gunung Impian Development Sdn Bhd; JLand Group; KEB Berhad; Matrix Concepts; Pinnacle Group; Tropicana Corporation Berhad; and UEM Sunrise Berhad. In addition, PropertyGuru.com.my and iProperty.com.my presented several titles for the first time this year. IIB Experience Centre (IIBEX) by Iskandar Investment Berhad received the inaugural Real Estate Ecosystem Catalyst Award. The Consistency Excellence Awards also made their debut, recognising companies with consecutive years of wins at the awards. Gunung Impian Development Sdn Bhd won the 4-Year Consistency Excellence Award. Meanwhile, the 3-Year Consistency Excellence Awards were presented to Armani Group; Astaka Padu Sdn Bhd; Berinda Group; Coronade Properties Sdn Bhd; Iskandar Investment Berhad; JLand Group; R&F Development Sdn Bhd; and Tropicana Corporation Berhad. Live selection process Winners of the competitive categories were selected during the Live Judging Days from 30 June to 2 July 2026 at the Amari Hotel Kuala Lumpur. The evaluation process, independently supervised by HLB Ler Lum Chew, saw a multi-disciplinary panel from Malaysia’s leading professional bodies assess an expanded lineup of categories. This year’s panel was chaired by Datuk Ar. Ezumi Harzani Ismail, president of the Malaysian Institute of Architects (PAM) from 2020 to 2022, and included Ir. Ashwin Thurairajah, executive director, GreenRE Sdn Bhd; YBrs. Sr. Haji Ishak Ismail, president, Malaysian Institute of Property & Facility Managers (MIPFM) 2023–2027; Ms. Janice Chin, senior director, Capital Markets, JLL Appraisal & Property Services Sdn Bhd; Prof. Dr. Ir. Jeffrey Chiang Choong Luin, president, The Institution of Engineers Malaysia (IEM) 2024–2026; Dato’ Sr. Lau Wai Seang, president, Royal Institution of Surveyors Malaysia (RISM) 2017–2018; TPr. Mazrina Dato’ Abdul Khalid, president, Malaysian Institute of Planners (MIP) 2025–2027; Assoc. Prof. LAr. Dr. Nor Atiah Ismail, president, Institute of Landscape Architects Malaysia (ILAM) 2024–2026; Adj. Prof. IDr. Norshafina Ibrahim, president, Malaysian Institute of Interior Designers (MIID) 2024–2026; Mr. Oliver Wee, president, Master Builders Association Malaysia (MBAM) 2024–2026; Ar. Sarly Adre Sarkum, chief executive officer, Green Building Index (GBI); Ar. Dr. Serina Hijjas, president, Malaysia Green Building Council (MGBC) 2023–2027; and Ms. Tan Hui Yin, partner, Tan Chap & Associates. Datuk Ar. Ezumi Harzani Ismail said: “Good design is the product of discipline, clarity of intent, and an understanding of how people inhabit space. What struck me most among this year’s winners was a shared design intelligence: sensitivity to context and climate, thoughtful handling of landscape and light, and a commitment to sustainability that goes beyond token gestures. From the elegant restraint of landed homes to the confident lines of high-rise towers, these projects show that Malaysian design has matured into something both internationally credible and distinctly our own. And with quality consistent across every tier, good design is not a privilege of the few but a standard we can deliver for all. On behalf of the judging panel, I congratulate every winner for raising the bar for Malaysian real estate.” Jules Kay, managing director of PropertyGuru Asia Property Awards and Events, said: “This year’s awardees share a commitment to thoughtful placemaking, sustainable design, and creating developments that enhance the way people live, work, and connect. From transformative township masterplans to beautifully crafted landed homes, this year’s winners show that excellence equals lasting value for communities. We are proud to celebrate developers that deliver value and quality to homebuyers. We also celebrate the individual leaders whose passion and foresight continue to inspire the industry. Together, these achievements set a benchmark for Malaysian real estate.” Winners may advance to the PropertyGuru Asia Property Awards Grand Final, recognising the Best in Asia on 11 December 2026 at The Athenee Hotel, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Bangkok.
